questions.question: What is the main purpose of a telescope's light-collecting area?
choices: Increasing an object's actual size
Creating the object's light
Gathering light from distant objects
Changing the object's orbit

questions.question: What does a spectroscope separate incoming light into?
choices: Individual planets
Layers of atmosphere by mass
Solid pieces of a star
Its component wavelengths

questions.question: What is a robotic space probe?
choices: An uncrewed spacecraft that collects information
A telescope lens made only of ice
A constellation used for navigation
A planet with no moons

questions.question: What is a rover designed to do?
choices: Collect only data from orbit without surface travel
Move across a surface while carrying instruments
Return every sample to Earth immediately
Serve only as a stationary relay above a planet

questions.question: What is remote sensing?
choices: Measuring only collected samples in a laboratory
Inferring properties without using any observations
Collecting information without directly contacting the target
Physically drilling into every target

questions.question: Which electromagnetic waves are detected by a radio telescope?
choices: Sound waves in space
Seismic waves
Ocean waves
Radio waves

questions.question: What does angular resolution describe?
choices: Ability to distinguish objects close together in apparent angle
The total mass of a telescope
The speed of a planet in its orbit
The number of instruments on a rocket

questions.question: Why are some telescopes placed above Earth's atmosphere?
choices: Space prevents all instrument errors
The atmosphere absorbs some wavelengths and distorts images
Stars emit light only outside the atmosphere
Gravity is completely absent there

questions.question: Why can a larger telescope reveal fainter objects under similar observing conditions?
choices: It always magnifies more even with identical optics
It makes the target emit more energy
It collects more light
It automatically removes detector noise completely

questions.question: How can spectroscopy help identify elements in a star?
choices: Elements are identified only by the object's apparent size
All elements emit an identical line pattern
Distance alone determines an object's composition
Elements produce characteristic patterns of spectral lines

questions.question: Why use observations at different wavelengths?
choices: Different wavelengths reveal different physical processes and materials
Every wavelength shows exactly the same structures
Only visible light can be detected by instruments
Using one wavelength removes all uncertainty

questions.question: Why can robotic missions be useful where human travel is difficult?
choices: They never require electrical energy
They collect data without requiring human life-support systems
They communicate instantaneously across all distances
They operate without any testing or calibration

questions.question: Why do spacecraft instructions sometimes need to be sent well in advance?
choices: Radio signals always arrive instantly after transmission
Communication delay occurs only inside computers
Signals take time to travel across space
All spacecraft are permanently beyond signal range

questions.question: What does calibration help establish for a telescope detector?
choices: The target's future orbit without observations
A guarantee of error-free results
A way to avoid taking any data
How its readings relate to known inputs

questions.question: Why can repeated observations strengthen a discovery claim?
choices: They help distinguish a real pattern from artifacts or chance
They guarantee every proposed explanation is correct
They remove the need to consider instrument errors
They make changing objects remain physically constant

questions.question: A camera records an unusual bright spot in only one exposure. What is a useful next step?
choices: Immediately declare a new planet
Check additional exposures and detector artifacts
Assume no instrument can make errors
Change the target's name without checking

questions.question: A satellite detects infrared radiation from a cloud hidden in visible light. What does this illustrate?
choices: The cloud emits only visible light
Infrared and visible observations must always look identical
Different wavelengths can reveal otherwise obscured features
The detector has changed the cloud's temperature by observing it

questions.question: A signal takes 10 minutes to travel from Earth to a spacecraft. Ignoring processing, what is the minimum command-and-response travel time?
choices: 5 minutes
10 minutes
100 minutes
20 minutes

questions.question: A detector gives a consistent offset when tested against known inputs. Which action directly addresses it?
choices: Apply a justified calibration correction
Assume every sky target has changed brightness
Take fewer measurements to hide the offset
Treat the offset as a new planet

questions.question: Two telescopes collect data at different wavelengths from the same object. Why compare the results?
choices: To guarantee that every difference is an instrument mistake
To build a fuller picture of its physical properties
To replace all measurements with one visible-light image
To make the object's properties independent of any model
